questions.question: What are `__init__` and `self` in Python?
questions.title: Understanding __init__ and self
questions.direct_answer: `__init__` initializes an instance after it has been created. `self` is the conventional name for the instance passed to an instance method, letting the method read and change that object's state.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know when initialization runs and why instance methods declare an explicit first parameter.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling `self` a keyword or saying `__init__` creates the object.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the difference between the call syntax and the function signature with one initialized object.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `__init__` runs automatically on a newly created instance.
It prepares the instance and must return `None`.
`self` refers to the instance receiving an instance-method call.
Python supplies the instance automatically when the method is called through it.
`self` is a strong naming convention, not a reserved keyword.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`__init__` is the instance initializer. Python calls it after a new instance has been created and passes in the arguments written in the class call. Its usual job is to place the object in a valid starting state by assigning attributes or checking input.

`self` is the conventional name for the current instance. In `def __init__(self, name)`, the caller writes `User("Mina")`; Python supplies the new object as `self` and `"Mina"` as `name`. The same rule applies to other instance methods.

For example, `self.name = name` stores the supplied value on that one `User`. A later `user.rename("Meera")` can update the same object through `self.name`. Another `User` keeps its own name.

`self` is not a keyword, but changing the name would make normal Python code harder to read. `__init__` also does not create the instance and cannot return a replacement object; object creation belongs to `__new__`. For most application classes, defining `__init__` is all that is needed.

sections.title: Initialization is the second half of construction
sections.content:
Calling a class uses Python's construction protocol. A new object is obtained first, and initialization follows only when the created value is an instance of the class being called. The initializer receives that object plus the caller's remaining arguments.

Assignments through the first parameter establish instance attributes. Nothing special happens because the parameter is spelled `self`; method binding supplies the receiver by position. The conventional name makes ownership visible in expressions such as `self.email` and `self.activate()`.

An initializer should leave the object ready to use. It can reject invalid input by raising an exception, but it must not return a non-`None` value. Alternative constructors are usually class methods that prepare or parse arguments and then call the class normally, preserving this initialization path.

sections.title: Arguments in a class call
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C[User Mina] --> N[Create a new User instance]
  N --> I[Call __init__ with instance and Mina]
  I --> A[Assign self.name]
  A --> R[Return the initialized object]
```

questions.question: What is the difference between `__new__` and `__init__` in Python?
questions.title: __new__ vs __init__
questions.direct_answer: `__new__` creates and returns an instance, while `__init__` receives an already-created instance and initializes it. Most classes customize only `__init__`; `__new__` is mainly needed for unusual creation rules or immutable subclasses.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can accurately separate allocation from initialization without overusing advanced hooks.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling both methods constructors or forgetting that `__new__` must return the object to use.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention immutable subclasses as the practical case where creation must happen before initialization.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `__new__` receives the class and returns a new object.
`__init__` receives that object and prepares its state.
If `__new__` returns another type, the original class's `__init__` is not called.
Ordinary mutable classes almost always need only `__init__`.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`__new__` and `__init__` are different stages of creating an object. `__new__` is called with the class and must return the object that will become the result. If that result is an instance of the class, Python then calls `__init__` on it.

`__init__` does not create or replace the object. It receives the existing instance and sets its initial state, and it must return `None`. That is why a normal business class defines `__init__` but rarely defines `__new__`.

A common use for `__new__` is subclassing an immutable type. For example, an uppercase `str` subclass must change the text before `str` creates the value, so `__new__` can call `super().__new__(cls, value.upper())`. There is no mutable string state for `__init__` to rewrite afterward.

`__new__` also appears in controlled creation patterns such as caching instances, but those designs affect identity and can surprise callers. My default is to keep construction ordinary and use a class method as a named factory unless creation itself truly must be customized.

sections.title: The object exists before it can be initialized
sections.content:
The class call is coordinated by the class's metaclass. At the class level, Python asks for a new value and then decides whether it should run that class's initializer. `object.__new__` supplies the standard creation behaviour for most user-defined classes.

Creation matters for immutable values because their stored value is fixed when the object is made. A subclass of `str`, `tuple`, or `int` cannot wait until initialization to replace that core value. Its `__new__` method delegates to the immutable base with the final data.

Returning a value that is not an instance of the requested class stops that class's initialization step. This power is why `__new__` should stay rare in beginner application code. Named class-method factories usually express parsing, validation, and alternative inputs more clearly while still following normal construction.

sections.title: Creation and initialization have separate contracts
sections.content:
| Detail | `__new__` | `__init__` |
|---|---|---|
| First parameter | The class, usually `cls` | The instance, usually `self` |
| Main job | Create and return an object | Initialize existing state |
| Return | An object | Must return `None` |
| Order | First | After successful creation |
| Common use | Immutable subclass or special identity rule | Nearly every ordinary class |
